summary: The bridge at Charenton crossed the Marne just above its confluence with the Seine, carrying the road south-east out of Paris. The present bridge carries the N6 between Charenton-le-Pont and Alfortville.

One of the oldest crossing points in Paris. The stone bridge of 1500–1512, lined with houses on both sides, is the one drawn here; it was replaced in 1853 by the present bridge, whose arches were reduced from five to three in 1912.

The 'little bridge' between the Île de la Cité and the Left Bank, on the line of the old Roman road. It was rebuilt many times; the present bridge dates from 1853 and was renamed Petit-Pont–Cardinal-Lustiger in 2013.
Named after the money-changers who kept their shops on it. The bridge on this map, lined with houses, linked the Cité to the Grand Châtelet; the present bridge dates from 1858–1860.
A bridge built over a row of water mills, just downstream of the Pont au Change. It collapsed in 1596; its successor, the Pont Marchand, burned in 1621 and was never rebuilt.
Links the Left Bank (place Saint-Michel) to the Île de la Cité. The bridge on the map was lined with houses; the present bridge was built in 1857.

A cluster of royal buildings that grew from the 14th century north of today's place des Vosges. Louis XII and Henri II both died here. After Henri II's death in 1559 Catherine de' Medici abandoned it; it was sold off and demolished, and the place Royale (place des Vosges) was laid out on part of its grounds.
An old town house in the Saint-Paul quarter, at what is now 16 rue Charlemagne. It was demolished in 1891.

The queen's lodgings in the Hôtel Saint-Pol, the rambling royal residence that Charles V assembled from four properties in 1361–1365. The estate was broken up and built over from 1544, which created the rue Neuve-Saint-Paul (rue Charles-V), the rue des Lions-Saint-Paul and the rue de la Cerisaie.

The seat of the Paris city government since 1357, on the place de Grève. The Renaissance building begun in 1533 was still unfinished when this map was made. It was burned during the Commune in 1871 and rebuilt in the same style.
A small fortress guarding the Left Bank end of the Petit-Pont, the counterpart of the Grand Châtelet on the Right Bank. It served as a prison and was demolished in 1782.

The fortress at the Right Bank end of the Pont au Change, built by Louis VI where the rue Saint-Denis met the river. It housed the court and prison of the Prévôté of Paris. It was demolished in 1802–1810; the place du Châtelet now occupies its site.
The clock tower at the north-east corner of the royal palace, now part of the Palais de Justice and the Conciergerie. Its clock was the first public clock in Paris.

The part of the royal palace of the Cité that became a prison in 1370, when the kings stopped living there. Two great medieval halls survive. During the Revolution, Marie-Antoinette and some 2,780 other prisoners were held and tried here.

The palace of the kings of France from the 10th to the 14th century, at the west end of the Île de la Cité. After the kings left, it remained the seat of the highest courts, as it still is: the Palais de Justice stands on the site and incorporates the Conciergerie and the Sainte-Chapelle.
The royal court of accounts, which audited the Crown's finances, the ancestor of today's Cour des comptes. Its building stood in the palace precinct and burned in 1737.

The town house of the abbots of Cluny, rebuilt in 1485–1510 next to the ruins of the Roman baths. It is one of the few medieval town houses left in Paris and now houses the Musée de Cluny, the national museum of the Middle Ages.
The royal mint stood here, near the rue de la Monnaie that is named after it. In 1775 the mint moved to its present building on the quai de Conti, on the Left Bank.
The prison of the bishops of Paris from 1222, later a royal prison, at what is now 19 rue Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois. It was demolished in 1783.

The town house of the dukes of Bourbon, facing the east gate of the medieval Louvre. The king confiscated it around 1523 and most of it was destroyed in 1525; its chapel and great hall, later used as a theatre by Molière, survived until 1660, when they made way for the Louvre colonnade.
The archbishops of Rouen had their Paris house here; 'Rohan' is a corruption of 'Rouen'. The courtyards of the Cour de Rohan, off the cour du Commerce-Saint-André, still survive.

In 1550 the medieval castle of the Louvre was being transformed: Pierre Lescot's Renaissance wing was begun in 1546 for François I. The palace grew for three more centuries and became a museum in 1793.
A great town house on the Left Bank, built against Philip Augustus's city wall, whose corner tower was the Tour de Nesle. The Institut de France and the Monnaie de Paris stand on its site.
A Cistercian abbey east of the city, around which the faubourg Saint-Antoine grew up. The Hôpital Saint-Antoine (12th arrondissement) now occupies its buildings.

A monastery of the Celestine order founded in the 14th century near the Bastille. After Saint-Denis it was the most important royal burial place in France: many princes were buried in its church. It has completely disappeared.

An old collegiate church at the southern exit of Paris, on the boundary of today's 5th and 13th arrondissements. It appears on many historic plans of Paris, including this one. Most of it was destroyed in the early 19th century; the last remains disappeared in 1874.
The parish church of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, in what is now the Croulebarbe quarter of the 13th arrondissement. It has disappeared.

A convent of Poor Clares founded in 1289 in the faubourg Saint-Marcel at the request of Queen Marguerite de Provence. The rue de Julienne, the rue Pascal and the rue des Cordelières were laid out across its grounds.

A priory founded by the sergeants-at-arms of the royal guard to commemorate the victory of Bouvines (1214). It was demolished at the end of the 18th century; the place du Marché-Sainte-Catherine was laid out on its site.

The parish church of the royal Hôtel Saint-Pol, on the rue Saint-Paul at the corner of today's rue Neuve-Saint-Pierre. It became a parish in 1125 and the royal parish in the 14th century; it was demolished in 1796–1799.
A convent on the rue de l'Ave-Maria in the Saint-Gervais quarter. It has disappeared; the street keeps its name.
The parish church of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, at 141 rue Mouffetard, built between the 15th and 18th centuries. It still serves as a parish church.

The headquarters of the Knights Templar in France, later the main house of the Hospitallers of Saint John. Until the Revolution the Temple enclosure kept its own jurisdiction inside Paris; Louis XVI was imprisoned in its keep. The square du Temple occupies part of its site.

Founded in the 1530s as the first Paris institution devoted solely to foundlings; the children were dressed in red. It became a barracks in 1808. The quarter and the Marché des Enfants-Rouges keep its name.

An abbey of canons regular founded in the 12th century by William of Champeaux. Within a few decades it became one of the great centres of theology and philosophy in medieval Europe. It was demolished after the Revolution; the Jussieu university campus stands on its site.

The church of the Billettes friars, at 24 rue des Archives. The present church was built in 1754–1758, but its cloister of the early 15th century survives: it is the only medieval cloister left in Paris. Today it is a Lutheran church.
The cemetery of the parish church of Saint-Jean-en-Grève, behind the Hôtel de Ville. It disappeared with the church, which was demolished in 1797–1800.

The church on the place Saint-Gervais, east of the Hôtel de Ville. The present Gothic church was built from 1494 and its classical façade added in 1616–1621, so in 1550 it was a building site. It is still a parish church.
A parish church near the Hôtel de Ville, first the baptismal chapel of nearby Saint-Gervais. It became a parish in 1212, was rebuilt in 1326 and was demolished in 1797–1800.
The cemetery of the parish of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs, on the rue Beaubourg. It has disappeared; the rue du Cimetière-Saint-Nicolas (now part of rue Chapon) was named after it.
The enclosure of the canons of Saint-Merri around their church. The rue du Cloître-Saint-Merri keeps its name.

The church of Saint-Merri on the rue Saint-Martin, by the Centre Pompidou, named after the abbot Médéric. The present Flamboyant Gothic church was built in 1500–1550, so it was brand new when this map was made.
A charitable institution beside the Hôtel de Ville that took in poor and abandoned children. It has disappeared.
The canons' quarter of Notre-Dame, occupying the north-east quarter of the Île de la Cité between today's rue d'Arcole and the quai aux Fleurs. A few of its old houses survive in the rue Chanoinesse.

A small church just behind the apse of Notre-Dame, on the site of today's square Jean-XXIII. It was the fifth station on the pilgrimage route from Paris to the basilica of Saint-Denis. It was demolished in the early 19th century.
A Cistercian college of the old University of Paris, built from 1248. Until the Revolution it housed monks studying in Paris. Its great Gothic hall survives and is used today as a cultural centre.

The church on the corner of the rue des Bernardins and the rue Saint-Victor. The present church was built from the second half of the 17th century on the site of a 13th-century church, and only finished in 1937.

The parish church of the montagne Sainte-Geneviève, next to the Panthéon. It replaced a 13th-century church and was built from the end of the 15th century to 1624, so the map shows it under construction.

An Augustinian abbey on the montagne Sainte-Geneviève, founded on the tomb of the patron saint of Paris. Several of its buildings, including the Tour Clovis, survive as the Lycée Henri-IV; the Panthéon was built as its new church.

The church of the faubourg Saint-Laurent, on the old Roman road north from Paris (today's rue du Faubourg-Saint-Martin). It still stands, at the junction of the boulevards de Strasbourg and de Magenta.
The church of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs on the rue Saint-Martin, built in five stages between 1420 and 1620, mostly in Flamboyant Gothic. It is still a parish church.

A priory founded in 1059 and given to the monks of Cluny in 1079; it became the most important Cluniac house after Cluny itself. Its church and refectory survive as part of the Musée des Arts et Métiers.
The chapel and hospital of the guild of minstrels and musicians, on the rue Saint-Martin. It has disappeared.
A large parish church founded in the 12th century and enlarged in the 14th and 16th centuries. It was demolished at the end of the 18th century; only its bell tower survives, the Tour Saint-Jacques.
A parish church on the Île de la Cité, near the river. It has disappeared.
A church on the Île de la Cité, behind Saint-Éloi, near the Palais de Justice. It has disappeared.
A parish church on the Île de la Cité. It has disappeared.
A small church on the Île de la Cité dedicated to Saint Genevieve, on what is now the parvis of Notre-Dame. It has disappeared.
A parish church on the Île de la Cité. It has disappeared.
The cathedral of Paris, begun in 1163 under bishop Maurice de Sully. It was already almost 400 years old when this map was made. It survived the fire of April 2019 and reopened in December 2024.

The oldest hospital in Paris, traditionally founded by bishop Saint Landry around 650. In 1550 it stood on the south side of the parvis, with buildings reaching across the small arm of the Seine. It was rebuilt on the north side of the parvis in 1867–1878.

A small medieval church on the Left Bank, in the square René-Viviani facing Notre-Dame. One of the oldest churches in Paris, it has been used by the Melkite Greek Catholic Church since the end of the 19th century.
The Great Carmelite convent next to the place Maubert, at the foot of the rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Geneviève. It has disappeared; the 5th arrondissement police station stands on its site.
A house of the Knights Hospitaller of Saint John on the Left Bank, where the rue de Latran is today. Its buildings were demolished in the mid-19th century.
A church on the montagne Sainte-Geneviève, in use from the 12th century until the Revolution. A few traces survive.
A church at the corner of the rue Saint-Jacques and the old rue Saint-Étienne-des-Grès (now rue Cujas). It has disappeared.
The church on the rue Saint-Jacques at the corner of the rue de l'Abbé-de-l'Épée. The present church was built in 1630–1685, replacing the older chapel of the hospital shown on this map.

In 1550 a priory of Notre-Dame-des-Champs stood here, south of the city. In 1603 it became the first convent of the Discalced Carmelites in Paris, which attracted nuns from the high nobility. It was closed at the Revolution and demolished in 1797.

The leper house of Saint-Lazare, in a large enclosure north of the city, in today's 10th arrondissement. From 1632 it was the headquarters of Vincent de Paul's congregation, and after the Revolution a prison.
The cemetery of the hospital of the Trinité, on the rue Saint-Denis. It has disappeared.
A hostel for pilgrims on the way to Santiago de Compostela, in the block between the rues Saint-Denis, Mauconseil, Mondétour and du Cygne. It was demolished in 1823.
A 13th-century church at 92 rue Saint-Denis. It is still a parish church.
A Benedictine abbey on the rue Saint-Denis. The monks moved out in 1572 and it has disappeared.
A church and hospice of the Holy Sepulchre on the rue Saint-Denis. It has disappeared.

The largest cemetery in Paris, by the Halles, named after the church of the Holy Innocents at its corner. It was closed in 1780 and the remains were moved to the Catacombs. The place Joachim-du-Bellay now covers it; the Renaissance Fontaine des Innocents, carved in 1549, stands in the middle.
A church near the Halles. It has disappeared; the place Sainte-Opportune keeps its name.
A hospital at the corner of the rue Saint-Denis and the rue des Lombards, where nuns sheltered poor women and buried the unclaimed dead. It was demolished in 1853.
A small church beside the Grand Châtelet. It was demolished in 1684 when the Châtelet was enlarged.
A parish church on the Île de la Cité, rebuilt in the 15th century and demolished at the end of the 18th century.
The parish church of the royal palace on the Île de la Cité, facing the palace across the rue de la Barillerie. It has disappeared.
A convent church on the Île de la Cité, later the church of the Barnabites, on the site now occupied by the Préfecture de police (2 rue de Lutèce).

The palace chapel built for Saint Louis to house the Crown of Thorns and other relics of the Passion that he acquired from 1239; it was consecrated in 1248. Its upper chapel is famous for its stained glass. The label was added by hand on the Basel copy of this map.
A chapel in the courtyard of the royal palace on the Île de la Cité. It has disappeared.
A Flamboyant Gothic church in the Latin Quarter, near the Seine, with the only surviving medieval charnel-house cloister in Paris. It is still a parish church.

The Paris house of the Trinitarian friars, known as Mathurins, from the early 13th century until 1790. It occupied the block now bounded by the rue Saint-Jacques, the boulevard Saint-Germain, the Hôtel de Cluny and the rue Du Sommerard.
An ancient church on the rue Saint-Jacques, founded in the 6th century. It was demolished in 1831 for the Théâtre du Panthéon, which in turn made way for the rue des Écoles in 1854.

A church built in 1427 at the corner of the rue de la Harpe and the rue des Cordeliers (now rue de l'École-de-Médecine). It was the religious centre of the surgeons who founded the Academy of Surgery. It was demolished around 1836.

The great Dominican convent of the rue Saint-Jacques, founded in the early 13th century. It gave the Dominicans their French name, Jacobins, after the street. Thomas Aquinas taught here. It has disappeared.

A convent of nuns who first served the hospital of Saint-Gervais and took in reformed prostitutes; their house on the rue Saint-Denis, just inside the Porte Saint-Denis, appears here. It has disappeared; the rue d'Alexandrie was the rue des Filles-Dieu.
A parish church on the rue Saint-Denis. It has disappeared; the rue Saint-Sauveur keeps its name.

The chapel of the goldsmiths' guild, dedicated to Saint Eligius, founded in the early 15th century and rebuilt in the mid-16th century — just when this map was made. It was destroyed at the end of the 18th century; traces of its façade survive at 8 rue des Orfèvres.
A parish church on the place Saint-André-des-Arts, demolished in the early 19th century. The square was laid out on its site.

The great Franciscan convent founded with the support of Saint Louis, in the Latin Quarter. During the Revolution it was the seat of the Cordeliers club. Only its refectory survives, at 15 rue de l'École-de-Médecine.
A Carthusian monastery founded in 1257 at Vauvert with the support of Saint Louis, south of the city. It was demolished in 1796–1800; part of its grounds is now in the Jardin du Luxembourg.
The parish church of the Halles. The present church, the third largest in Paris, was begun in 1532 and completed in 1637; this map still shows the older church it replaced.
A convent of reformed women, the Filles Pénitentes, founded at the end of the 15th century. In 1572 they moved to the former abbey of Saint-Magloire on the rue Saint-Denis.
The parish church of the Louvre, facing the palace's east front. It has been called the 'parish of the artists'. Its bell gave the signal for the Saint Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572.
A large Augustinian friary on the Left Bank by the Seine, whose name survives in the quai and rue des Grands-Augustins. It was destroyed during the Revolution.

A chapel on the slope of Montmartre, on the spot where Saint Denis was believed to have been martyred. It belonged to the abbey of Montmartre. A modern chapel of the Martyrdom stands near the site, on the rue Yvonne-Le-Tac.
A collegiate church on the rue Saint-Honoré, in today's 1st arrondissement. It has disappeared; buildings of the Ministry of Culture stand on its site.
The church of the faubourg Saint-Germain. The present church, the second largest in Paris, was begun in 1646 to replace the church shown here.

The hospital for 300 (fifteen score: quinze-vingts) blind people founded by Saint Louis, on the rue Saint-Honoré near the Louvre. In 1780 it moved to the faubourg Saint-Antoine (28 rue de Charenton), where it is still the national eye hospital.
A collegiate church near the Louvre. It was demolished in 1739 and replaced by the church of Saint-Louis-du-Louvre, which has also disappeared.

A Benedictine abbey founded in the mid-6th century by the Merovingian king Childebert I and Saint Germain, bishop of Paris. The abbey church survives as the oldest church in Paris; the monastery buildings have gone.
A convent of Minim friars, known as the Bonshommes, in the village of Nigeon (Chaillot), west of Paris. It has disappeared.
A college of the University of Paris founded by Cardinal Jean Lemoine (d. 1313). The rue du Cardinal-Lemoine keeps its name.
A college founded in 1353 on the rue Bordelle (now rue Descartes) by Pierre Becoud, whose name was corrupted into 'Boncourt'. It was later united with the college of Navarre.
A college of the University of Paris on the rue de la Montagne-Sainte-Geneviève, also called the college de la Marche-Winville. It has disappeared.

A college founded in 1304 by Queen Joan I of Navarre, wife of Philip IV, on the montagne Sainte-Geneviève. It was one of the most prestigious colleges of the university. Its site was later taken over by the École polytechnique.
A college of the University of Paris near the Porte Saint-Victor. It has disappeared.
A college for students from the diocese of Cornouaille in Brittany. Its bursars were first housed at the college du Plessis; in 1374 a house was bought for them on the rue du Plâtre (now rue Domat).
A college of the University of Paris near the place Maubert. The philosopher Petrus Ramus was its principal in the 1540s–1560s.

A college founded in 1370 by Cardinal Jean de Dormans, bishop of Beauvais, on the rue du Clos-Bruneau (now rue Jean-de-Beauvais). Its Gothic chapel survives as the Romanian Orthodox church of Saint-Jean-de-Beauvais.
The 'Schools of Decretals', home of the faculty of canon law of the old University of Paris, on the rue Jean-de-Beauvais. The faculty was closed in 1793 and refounded in 1802 as the Paris law school.
A college founded in 1334 for poor students from Lombardy and the rest of Italy. It flourished until the 16th century and was later taken over by Irish priests (the college des Irlandais).

A small college on the montagne Sainte-Geneviève, founded in the mid-15th century by Nicolas Coqueret. Around 1547 the humanist Jean Dorat became its principal and taught Ronsard and Du Bellay here, the poets of the Pléiade.
A college on the rue Saint-Jacques next to the college of Clermont (Louis-le-Grand). Its buildings were demolished in 1864 for the northern part of the present Lycée Louis-le-Grand.
A college of the University of Paris from 1412 to 1762, founded by Guy de Roye, archbishop of Reims.
A college founded by Cardinal Philippe de Luxembourg, bishop of Le Mans, for ten students from his diocese.
A college of the University of Paris, belonging to the abbey of Marmoutier near Tours, on the rue Saint-Jacques next to the college du Plessis.

Founded in 1460 on the montagne Sainte-Geneviève; until it closed in 1999 it was the oldest school in Paris. Its rebuilt buildings now house the Bibliothèque Sainte-Barbe. Ignatius of Loyola and Francis Xavier studied here.
A college of the University of Paris at what is now 4 rue Cujas. It has disappeared.
A college of the University of Paris, also known as the college Saint-Michel. It has disappeared.
A college of the faculty of arts, known for its harsh discipline; Erasmus and Calvin studied here. The Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève was built on its site in 1844–1850.
A college of the University of Paris, also called the college de Torcy. It has disappeared.
A college of the University of Paris, founded in the 14th century by Gervais Chrétien, physician to Charles V. It has disappeared.
A college founded in 1280 on the rue de la Harpe and closed in 1793. The Lycée Saint-Louis stands on its site.
A college of the University of Paris, on the rue de la Harpe. It has disappeared.
A college founded in 1317 on the rue de la Harpe by Bernard de Farges, archbishop of Narbonne, for nine students from his diocese. The future Pope Clement VI studied here.

The college founded in 1257 by Robert de Sorbon with the support of Saint Louis, for students of theology. Its name came to stand for the whole faculty of theology. The present Sorbonne was rebuilt by Richelieu in the 17th century and again in 1885–1901.

A college founded in 1271 by Robert de Sorbon for poor students of the humanities and philosophy, nicknamed the 'little Sorbonne'. It was demolished in the 17th century to make room for the Sorbonne church.

A college of the University of Paris founded in the 13th century for monks of the order of Cluny. Its buildings were seized during the Revolution and disappeared in the 19th century, roughly between the place de la Sorbonne and the rue Cujas.
A medieval college of the University of Paris, later the college de Grandmont. The rue Mignon, laid out on its site, keeps its name.
A college of the University of Paris founded in 1331 by Queen Joan of Burgundy, on the rue des Cordeliers. The École de Médecine was built on its site.
A small college of the University of Paris on the rue Saint-Honoré, near the Louvre. The rue des Bons-Enfants keeps its name.

A bastion of the city wall of Charles V (built 1356–1383). Its eastern part was strengthened with bastions in the mid-16th century, around the time of this map; the wall was demolished in the 17th century and the Grands Boulevards follow its line.
The eastern gate of Paris, on the rue Saint-Antoine next to the Bastille, in the wall of Charles V. It stood from the mid-14th century until the late 18th century.

A fortress built in the 14th century to guard the Porte Saint-Antoine, later a state prison and a symbol of royal despotism. It was stormed on 14 July 1789 and completely demolished; the place de la Bastille covers its site.
The gate of the rue du Temple in the wall of Charles V (there was also an older gate of the same name in Philip Augustus's wall). It has disappeared; it stood near today's place de la République.
A gate of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, also called the Porte Saint-Marcel or Porte Bordet, on today's rue Descartes. It was built in the early 13th century and demolished in the 17th.
The gate of the rue Saint-Martin in the wall of Charles V. In 1674 Louis XIV replaced it with the triumphal arch of the Porte Saint-Martin, which stands near the site.
The southern gate of Philip Augustus's wall, on the rue Saint-Jacques, also called the Porte Notre-Dame-des-Champs. It led to the road to Orléans and Santiago de Compostela.
The gate of the rue Saint-Denis in the wall of Charles V, the ceremonial entrance of kings into Paris. In 1672–1673 Louis XIV replaced it with the triumphal arch of the Porte Saint-Denis.
A gate of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, also called the Porte d'Enfer or Porte Gibard. It was built in the early 13th century and demolished in the 17th.
A gate of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, near today's carrefour de l'Odéon. It was built in the 13th century and demolished in the 17th.
A gate of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, first called the Porte des Cordeliers, near today's carrefour de l'Odéon. It was built in the 13th century and demolished in the 17th.
The gate of the rue Montmartre in the wall of Charles V. There were three successive Porte Montmartre gates along the rue Montmartre as the city walls expanded; all have disappeared.

A corner tower of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, facing the Louvre across the Seine, built in the early 13th century. It is famous from the scandal of the Tour de Nesle (1314) and later legends. The east pavilion of the Institut de France stands on its site.

The western gate of Paris in the wall of Charles V, on the rue Saint-Honoré, leading towards Saint-Germain-en-Laye. There were three successive Porte Saint-Honoré gates as the walls expanded; all have disappeared.
A royal forest east of Paris, with the castle of Vincennes. With 995 hectares it is now the largest green space of Paris, in the 12th arrondissement.
France's longest river, the main tributary of the Seine. It joins the Seine between Charenton-le-Pont and Alfortville, at the top of this map.
The river of Paris. On this map it flows from the top (east) to the bottom (west).

An island in the Seine opposite the Arsenal, used for storing timber and hay. In 1843 the arm of the river separating it from the Right Bank was filled in; the boulevard Morland runs along its former channel.
The great royal gallows of Paris, on the hill of Montfaucon near today's place du Colonel-Fabien. It was in use from at least the 11th century to the reign of Louis XIII. Nothing of it remains.
A gate of the earliest medieval wall of the Right Bank, east of Saint-Gervais. Its name survives in the place Baudoyer.
Open ground at the eastern tip of the Île de la Cité, behind Notre-Dame, where the cathedral's builders stored stone. The square Jean-XXIII now occupies it.

A fortified tower at the riverside end of Philip Augustus's wall on the Left Bank, on the quai that keeps its name, roughly where the restaurant La Tour d'Argent stands. It was later used as a prison for galley convicts.

The Gobelin family of dyers had their works and mills on the Bièvre here from the 15th century. In 1601 Henri IV installed a tapestry workshop in their buildings, which became the royal Manufacture des Gobelins in 1662; it is still active at 42 avenue des Gobelins.
The garden of the royal palace at the western tip of the Île de la Cité. After the Pont Neuf was built (1578–1607) the place Dauphine was laid out on this ground.

In 1550 this was still an area of tile kilns (tuileries) outside the city wall. Catherine de' Medici began a palace here in 1564, with a garden; the palace burned in 1871, but the Jardin des Tuileries remains.
The 'clerks' meadow', the riverside meadow of the University's students west of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, notorious for brawls and duels. The rue du Pré-aux-Clercs (7th arrondissement) keeps its name.
The square in front of the Hôtel de Ville, called the place de Grève until 1803. It sloped down to a sandy river bank (grève) where boats unloaded; it was also the place of public executions.
A square at the foot of the montagne Sainte-Geneviève, one of the oldest market places of the Left Bank. The printer and humanist Étienne Dolet was burned here in 1546.
A cross at the corner of the rue Saint-Honoré and the rue de l'Arbre-Sec, also a place of execution. A public fountain stood here from the 16th century; it was rebuilt in 1776 and still stands.
A great annual fair held in the faubourg Saint-Germain from 1486 until the Revolution, first held in the 12th century. The Marché Saint-Germain stands on its site.
The pig market. It moved several times over the centuries; on this map it is in the faubourg Saint-Honoré, west of the city.

The great road east to the Porte Saint-Antoine and the Bastille, on the line of an old Roman road. It once ran from the rue des Barres to the place de la Bastille; the western stretch was renamed rue François-Miron in 1865.

Laid out across the gardens (the cherry orchard) of the royal Hôtel Saint-Pol when the estate was broken up from 1544, so it was brand new when this map was made. It has also been called rue Neuve-de-la-Cerisaie.

An old street by the Célestins convent, recorded in 1358 with the crude name 'Pute-y-Muse', which was softened over time into 'Petit-Musc'. Some 16th-century plans, like this one, call it the rue des Célestins.
A street of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, called the rue de la Barre in 1540. It was renamed after Scipion Sardini, an Italian banker who built a house here in the 1560s.
A street of the faubourg Saint-Marcel built in the 12th century. Its two parts, the rue de la Muette and the rue Permoulin, were later joined under the name rue du Fer-à-Moulin.
A street of dyers in the faubourg Saint-Marcel, by the Bièvre whose water they used. It is now part of the rue Saint-Hippolyte.

Named after the Cordelières convent, this was part of the old rue de Lourcine in the faubourg Saint-Marcel, created in the 12th century. It was split and renamed in the 20th century: rue Edouard-Quénu (1938), rue Broca and rue Léon-Maurice-Nordmann.
In the Marais, once called the rue Tougin and later part of the rue de Thorigny, now the rue de la Perle.

The rue de la Culture-Sainte-Catherine, which ran past the fields (culture) of the priory of Sainte-Catherine. It was renamed rue de Sévigné in 1867 after the letter-writer Madame de Sévigné, who lived at the Hôtel Carnavalet on this street.
The rue Percée ('pierced' street, cut through a block), called rue Percié by Guillot in 1300. It was renamed rue du Prévôt in 1877.
The street of the church of Saint-Paul, already in existence in the mid-14th century. It still runs from the quai to the rue Saint-Antoine.
A street along the inside of Philip Augustus's wall in the Saint-Paul quarter, earlier simply the rue des Jardins. A long stretch of the wall still stands along it.

Laid out from 1544 on the site of the Hôtel de Saint-Maur, part of the royal Hôtel Saint-Pol, as the rue Neuve-Saint-Paul. It was renamed rue Charles-V in 1864 after the king who built the Hôtel Saint-Pol.
A street of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, laid out in the early 13th century, known as the rue d'Orléans(-Saint-Marcel). It was renamed after the naturalist Louis Daubenton.
The rue du Grand-Chantier ran between the rue des Haudriettes and the rue Pastourelle. It became part of the rue des Archives, named after the National Archives in the nearby Hôtel de Soubise.

In the early 14th century the rue de l'Échelle du Temple, in 1450 the rue des Deux-Portes, later the rue des Quatre-Fils-Aymon, after the heroes of a medieval romance — probably from a shop sign. The name has since been shortened to rue des Quatre-Fils.
The rue de Paradis in the Marais, between the rue Vieille-du-Temple and the rue des Archives. It was joined to the rue des Francs-Bourgeois in 1868.

Already mentioned in 13th-century deeds as the 'old rue du Temple'. Over the centuries it was also called rue de la Couture du Temple and rue Barbette, after the Porte Barbette in Philip Augustus's wall.
The rue des Poulies, near the Marais. The rue des Francs-Bourgeois, named after almshouses whose residents were exempt from taxes, absorbed several neighbouring streets in 1868 and 1893.
Probably a second label on the same street as the 'Vieille rue du Temple' nearby; the poet Guillot called it simply the rue du Temple in 1300.
The rue des Singes in the Marais, probably named after a shop sign. It was made part of the rue des Guillemites in 1868.
Already built up and bearing this name in 1230. It is the heart of the Pletzl, the historic Jewish quarter of the Marais.
Recorded as the rue de l'Écofle in 1233; an escoufle is a kite (the bird of prey), probably from a shop sign. The name evolved through Escoufle and Escoufles into Écouffes.
Recorded under many spellings — rue Payelle, Parelle, des Payens, de Guienne. On this map it is the rue des Paiens.

Named after Charles of Anjou, king of Sicily and brother of Saint Louis, who had a house here. In 1868 it absorbed the rue de Bercy-Saint-Jean, which this map labels separately as the rue Bouquetonne.
A short street in the Marais, the rue des Ballets or Ballays. It is now part of the rue Malher.
Built up by 1250 as the rue Renaut-le-Fèvre. In the 17th century it was called the rue Cloche-Percée — from a sign showing a pierced bell — and the name later became Cloche-Perce.

The street of the abbot of Jouy, who had his Paris house here in the 13th century; part of it was later called the rue de la Fausse-Poterne-Saint-Paul. The reading 'Petit Ioui' on the label is uncertain.
In existence in 1300, under names such as rue Frogier-l'Asnier and rue Forgier-l'Asnier, after a man who lived here; the name later became Geoffroy-l'Asnier.

A street near Saint-Gervais that ran down to the river: in 1257 the rue André-sur-l'Eau, then Garnier-sur-l'Yaue, the form on this map. Part of its old line became the allée des Justes-de-France in 2000.
In existence in 1182, named after the nuns of the abbey of Hyères (Yerres) who had their Paris house here; the label reads 'Nonnaindières'.
The rue Copeau, named after the mound of Coupeau (Copeau) where the Jardin des Plantes was later created. It was renamed in 1853 after the naturalist Lacépède.

The 'great street of Saint-Marcel', on the line of the Roman road from Lutetia south towards Italy. It was the main street of the faubourg Saint-Marcel, leading out from the Porte Bordelles; it is today's rue Mouffetard and its continuation.
The rue de la Croix, between the old rue Phélipeaux and the rue du Vertbois. It was joined with neighbouring streets in 1851 to form the rue Volta, named after the Italian physicist.
In existence in the early 15th century, named after the fountains supplied by the springs of Belleville; earlier simply the rue des Fontaines.
The rue Frépaux (also Fripaux), later the rue Phélipeaux, near the Temple. It was destroyed when the rue Réaumur was cut through at the end of the 19th century.
In 1282 the rue Richard-des-Poulies, later the rue Portefoin. In the 17th century it was also called the rue des Enfants-Rouges, after the orphanage nearby.
Recorded as the rue Jehan-de-Saint-Quentin in 1302 and as the rue Pastourelle around 1330, perhaps after a Roger Pastourel who owned land here.
In existence in 1292, then called the rue Robert-Bégon or Capon, later the rue du Coq; its eastern part was the rue du Cimetière-Saint-Nicolas until 1851.

The main road north from the Hôtel de Ville to the Temple enclosure. Its southern stretches had other names — rue des Coquilles, rue Barre-du-Bec, rue Sainte-Avoie — until they were all joined as the rue du Temple.
The eastern part of today's rue de Montmorency: in 1328 the 'ruelle au Villain', later the rue Cour-au-Villain or Courtauvillain. It was joined to the rue de Montmorency in the 19th century.
An old street of the Temple quarter, named after a Michel le Comte. During the Revolution (1793–1806) it was renamed after the deputy Michel Lepeletier.
Named after the Haudriettes, a community of widows founded by Étienne Haudry. In 1290 it was the rue Jehan-l'Huilier; it has also been called rue de l'Échelle-du-Temple.
A street opened by the Templars, first called the rue des Boucheries-du-Temple; it later took the name of the chapel of Braque, which stood on it.
Named after the 'white mantles', mendicant friars (Servites) who settled here in 1258. In the 13th century it was the rue de la Parcheminerie.
The rue du Puits in the Marais, named after a well. It was renamed in 1867 after Hugues Aubriot, provost of Paris under Charles V.
The rue de l'Homme-Armé ('street of the armed man', after a shop sign). It is now part of the rue des Archives.
In 1232 the rue de Lagny, called 'de la Grande Bretonnerie'. Its name comes from the priory of Sainte-Croix-de-la-Bretonnerie that stood on it.
In existence by the mid-12th century as the 'vicus Burgi Thibaudi', the street of Thibaud's borough. The label shows one of its many corrupted forms, 'Bouti Bourg'.
In the late 13th century the rue du Franc-Mourier (or Franc-Meurier); by 1644 it was already called the rue de Moussy.

The rue Bouquetonne, also called rue du Hoqueton. Under the name of rue de Bercy-Saint-Jean it was joined to the rue du Roi-de-Sicile in 1868. The Paris street register cites this map for the form 'Bouquetonne'.
In existence in the 13th century; in the 16th century it was the rue Chartron, 'called des Mauvais-Garçons' (of the bad boys), after the mercenaries who stayed here in the 1520s.
The rue du Coq-Saint-Jean, in the 13th century the rue André-Malet. It was destroyed when the rue de Rivoli was cut through; the remaining stub, the impasse du Coq, disappeared in 1904.
The weavers' street (tisserands), recorded as Tixeranderie in 1263. It ran from the rue Jean-Pain-Mollet to the place Baudoyer and was destroyed when the rue de Rivoli was cut through in the 1850s.

A street behind Saint-Jean-en-Grève with the earthy name of rue du Pet-au-Diable ('devil's fart'), after a boundary stone. Later called the rue du Tourniquet-Saint-Jean, it disappeared when the Hôtel de Ville was enlarged.
Named after the mill of the Barres; in 1250 the 'ruelle au Moulin des Barres', later the rue du Chevet-Saint-Gervais, as it runs behind the apse of Saint-Gervais.

In the 13th century the 'rue aux Moines de Longpont', after the monks of Longpont priory who owned property here, later simply the rue de Longpont. It was renamed in 1838 after Salomon de Brosse, architect of the façade of Saint-Gervais.

Recorded in 1212; first the rue de la Foulerie (fullers), then the rue de la Mortellerie (mortar-makers). It runs behind the Hôtel de Ville and was renamed accordingly; part of it was demolished in the 1850s.
A street along the inside of Philip Augustus's wall, first called the rue des Murs. In the 14th century it became the rue d'Arras, corrupted to 'rue Dras' and 'rue des Ras', the form on this map.
A short street between the rue Saint-Victor and the rue Traversine, called 'Verseille' by the poet Guillot in 1300. It was renamed rue Fresnel in 1864 and destroyed soon after for the rue Monge.
Another short street between the rue Saint-Victor and the rue Traversine, called the rue de la Fortune in 1540. It was destroyed when the rue Monge was cut through.

On the line of the Roman road south from Lutetia; in the mid-13th century the rue Bordet (later Bordelle), leading to the Porte Bordelles. René Descartes is said to have lived nearby; it was renamed after him.
In existence in 1540 as the rue des Poteries or des Pots (potteries), later the rue des Postes. It was renamed after the grammarian Charles-François Lhomond.
Recorded in 1546, so new at the time of this map. Its eastern part was the rue Neuve-Saint-Laurent; a stretch was demolished for the rue de Turbigo.
An old street of the Saint-Martin quarter, named after the mayor (maire) of the priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. The label spells it 'Au Mere'.
The rue Transnonain ('beyond the nuns'), now part of the rue Beaubourg. In 1834 it was the scene of a massacre of civilians by soldiers, made famous by Daumier's lithograph.
The minstrels' street: in 1225 the 'vicus Viellatorum', in 1300 the rue des Jugleurs (jugglers). It was absorbed by the rue Rambuteau in the 1840s.
A very old street, recorded in the 13th century, named after a man called Geoffroy l'Angevin. It survives next to the Centre Pompidou.
The rue de la Baudrerie (leather-workers). It is now part of the rue Brisemiche, beside the Centre Pompidou.
A small street near Saint-Merri whose name comes from a 13th-century owner, Pierre Oilart, corrupted into 'Pierre-au-Lard' (Peter the bacon). Part of it was closed in 1817.
The rue Neuve-Saint-Merri, recorded in the early 13th century. It is now the rue Saint-Merri, which runs past the Centre Pompidou.
One of the stretches of the rue de la Poterie (potters' street) near Saint-Merri. It is now part of the rue du Renard.
The rue de la Courroierie (strap-makers), later the rue des Cinq-Diamants. It is now part of the rue Quincampoix.
The rue de la Poterie (potters' street), east of Saint-Merri. In 1868 it became part of the rue du Renard.
In 1300 the port Saint-Landry, a landing place on the north bank of the Cité, later the rue du Port-Saint-Landry and the rue Basse-des-Ursins. It is now the rue des Ursins.
Named after the Bièvre: a branch of the river was diverted through here to the Seine in the 12th century. It has borne its name since 1250.
Named after the college of the Bernardins (Cistercians) that stands on it; first mentioned under this name in 1427. Its southern part was the rue Saint-Nicolas-du-Chardonnet.

The road from the place Maubert to the abbey of Saint-Victor, which existed when the abbey was founded in the 12th century. The boulevard Saint-Germain, the rue Monge and the rue des Écoles absorbed parts of it.
The rue Saint-Nicolas-du-Chardonnet, named after the church. It is now part of the rue des Bernardins.
In the 13th century the rue Alexandre-Langlois (Alexander the Englishman), in 1540 the rue du Paon. It was destroyed when the rue des Écoles was cut through in the 1850s.

A short street between the rue Saint-Victor and the rue Traversine, recorded as 'Pavée' in 1243 and later called rue du Mûrier and rue Pavée-d'Andouilles. It was destroyed when the rue des Écoles was cut through.
Perhaps the rue Clopin, near the college of Navarre; the reading of the label is uncertain. Part of the rue Clopin was absorbed by the École polytechnique in 1809, and the rest has also disappeared.
On the line of the Roman road south from Lutetia, the street climbing the montagne Sainte-Geneviève. It has been called rue Sainte-Geneviève, rue du Mont and rue des Boucheries.
In existence in 1250; the name probably comes from the gravel (gravier) of the area. The western part was the rue Jean-Robert until it was joined to the rue des Gravilliers.
The rue du Cimetière-Saint-Nicolas, along the cemetery of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs, opened around 1220. In 1851 it was made part of the rue Chapon.

Its western part was called, from the 14th century, the street of the lord of Montmorency, who had his town house here. The house that the scribe and bookseller Nicolas Flamel built in 1407, at no. 51, is one of the oldest houses in Paris.
Partly built up by 1250, when it was called the rue Garnier-Saint-Ladre; 'Saint-Ladre' is an old form of Saint-Lazare.

The rue des Petits-Champs in the Saint-Martin quarter, renamed rue Brantôme in 1864. It disappeared in the clearance of the Beaubourg plateau; a modern rue Brantôme near the Centre Pompidou revives the name.
Recorded in 1210, written 'Quinquempoit' by the poet Guillot in 1300; the label splits the name into 'Qui quen poix'. In 1719–1720 it was the centre of John Law's speculative bubble.
The street of the bathhouses (étuves): in 1300 the rue des Estuves, later the rue des Vieilles-Étuves-Saint-Martin. It disappeared in the clearance of the Beaubourg plateau.

The ancient Roman road north from the Seine, the cardo of Lutetia, leading to the abbey of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. Its southern end had other names (rue des Arcis, rue Planche-Mibray) until they were joined into the rue Saint-Martin.
The rue de la Vieille-Courroierie (strap-makers), called the rue des Cinq-Diamants from 1536. It is now the southern part of the rue Quincampoix.
Recorded as the rue Marivas in 1280, later the rue Marivaux. It was renamed in 1851 after Nicolas Flamel, the scribe and bookseller who lived here and whom legend made an alchemist.
A small street near Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie, named after a man called Jean Pain-Mollet ('soft bread'). It was destroyed when the rue de Rivoli was cut through.

Called the rue de la Juiverie in the Middle Ages, when the Jewish community lived here. The present street of the same name only partly follows its line; the rest was destroyed by the avenue Victoria and the rue de Rivoli.
The cutlers' street, created at the end of the 12th century and widened in 1564. Earlier names include rue de la Vieille-Oreille and rue Guillori.
The basket-makers' street (vanniers), named in 1252, running from the place de Grève to the rue Saint-Martin. It was destroyed when the avenue Victoria was built in the 1850s.
The tanners' street, running from the place de Grève to the rue Saint-Martin, earlier the rue de l'Écorcherie (flaying). It was destroyed when the avenue Victoria was built.
A street on the north side of the Cité, called Glateingni by Guillot in 1300 and also the rue du Val-d'Amour, as it was a street of brothels. It was destroyed in 1865 to build the new Hôtel-Dieu.
Built in 1163, when Notre-Dame was begun, to bring building materials to the cathedral; it ran from the parvis to the rue du Marché-Palu. It was absorbed into the enlarged parvis in the 19th century.

The rue du Pavé (de la place Maubert), also called the rue d'Amboise, between the rue de la Bûcherie and the rue Galande. It was merged with the place Maubert from 1806 to 1912 and is now the rue Frédéric-Sauton.
In existence in the early 13th century; in 1247 the street of the plasterers (rue des Plâtriers), later the rue du Plâtre. It was renamed after the jurist Jean Domat.
The rue des Noyers (walnut trees) on the Left Bank. It was absorbed by the boulevard Saint-Germain in the 1850s.
Opened as the rue du Clos-Bruneau and later called rue Saint-Hilaire (1322); it takes its present name from the Carmelite convent on the place Maubert.
Opened in the early 14th century on the Clos Bruneau, a vineyard. It takes its name from the college of Dormans-Beauvais, whose chapel still stands on it.
The rue du Clos-Bruneau, named after a vineyard on the slope of the montagne Sainte-Geneviève; in 1243 the rue Judas. It was mostly destroyed by the boulevard Saint-Germain.

The ancient Roman road south from the Seine, the cardo of Lutetia, and the start of the pilgrimage road to Santiago de Compostela. In the Middle Ages its stretches had many names, such as the grand'rue du Petit-Pont.
The rue des Cholets, named after the college of that name, earlier the rue Saint-Symphorien. It was closed by royal order in 1845.
The rue Saint-Étienne-des-Grès, named after the church at its corner with the rue Saint-Jacques. It became part of the rue Cujas in 1865.
In existence in the early 13th century, called the rue Guérin-Boucel; the name evolved into Guérin-Boisseau.
Its old name was the rue d'Arnetal, written 'Garnetal' here, which later became Greneta. In 1868 the neighbouring rue du Renard-Saint-Sauveur and rue Beaurepaire were joined to it.
The old Roman road to Flanders and the abbey of Saint-Denis, lined with houses by 1134. It was the main street of the Right Bank and the route of royal entries into Paris.
The street of the 'abbot's borough', the land of the abbey of Saint-Martin-des-Champs. It was cut in two by the boulevard de Sébastopol.
A rue Pavée (paved street) near Saint-Sauveur, also called rue Pavée-Saint-Sauveur. It is now part of the rue Tiquetonne.
The rue du Petit-Lion(-Saint-Sauveur), between the rue Saint-Denis and the rue Dussoubs, recorded as the rue du Lion-d'Or in 1360. It is now part of the rue Tiquetonne.

In existence in the 13th century between the rue Saint-Martin and the rue Saint-Denis. The name is not about bears: it was the rue as Oues, the street of geese (oies), where poultry was roasted and sold.
The street of the hemp merchants (chanvre), between the Halles and the rue Saint-Denis. It was absorbed by the rue Rambuteau in the 1840s.
An old street of the Halles, recorded in 1184. Its name probably comes from a shop sign showing a preacher.
Built up by 1183; the cossonniers were poultry and egg dealers. The label's 'Cochonnerie' (pig street) is a popular corruption of the name.
The rue aux Fers, along the south side of the cemetery of the Innocents; Henri IV was assassinated in its extension, the rue de la Ferronnerie, in 1610. It became part of the rue Berger in 1864.
Cited in a deed of 1275 as the 'vicus Alberici Carnificis', the street of Aubry the butcher. The label garbles the name into 'Bribouche'.
By 1229 the rue de la Ferronnerie (ironmongers), earlier the rue de la Charronnerie (cartwrights). Henri IV was assassinated here by Ravaillac on 14 May 1610.
The rue Troussevache, recorded in 1248, between the rue Quincampoix and the rue Saint-Denis. It was renamed after Gabriel Nicolas de La Reynie, the first lieutenant-general of police of Paris.
Named after the Lombard (Italian) bankers and money-lenders who settled here in the Middle Ages. In 1877 the rue de l'Aiguillerie was joined to it.
The street of the helmet-makers (heaume = helmet), recorded in 1300. It was destroyed when the rue de Rivoli was cut through in the 1850s.
The soap-makers' street, named in the early 14th century. It was destroyed when the rue de Rivoli was cut through.

Probably the rue de la Saunerie (salt), between the quai de la Mégisserie and the rue Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois; the label reads 'de la Serpente'. It disappeared when the place du Châtelet was enlarged.

The rue du Crucifix-Saint-Jacques, by the church of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie, later merged into the rue Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie. It disappeared when the rue de Rivoli and the square of the Tour Saint-Jacques were laid out.
The street of the washerwomen of Sainte-Opportune, in existence in the early 13th century; it once ran down to the river. Its southern end was renamed rue Édouard-Colonne in 1912.
The furriers' street on the north side of the Cité, recorded in 1183. In 1786 a royal edict ordered its houses demolished to widen the quai; it disappeared completely in 1860.

The rue de la Vieille-Draperie (old cloth market) in the Cité, recorded as the rue de la Draperie in 1293. This map labels it 'rue de la Verrerie' by mistake, as does Ducerceau's plan of 1555. It is now the rue de Lutèce.
The street of the cobblers (savetiers) in the Cité, later the rue Saint-Éloi. It disappeared in the rebuilding of the Cité in the 1860s.
A street in the Cité running from the rue de la Cité to the rue de la Barillerie, opposite the palace. Tradition places Saint Marcel's birth here. It was demolished around 1860.
In existence in 1200 as the rue de Laas; by 1284 it was already the rue de la Huchette. In the 17th century it was known for its roasting shops (rue des Rôtisseurs).

A short street between the rue de la Harpe and the rue Hautefeuille, called Popée in 1200 and Poupée in 1300. It was destroyed when the boulevard Saint-Michel was cut through. The label was added by hand on the Basel copy.
In 1273 the street of the scribes (rue des Écrivains), in the 15th century the street of the parchment-makers, close to the University. It still exists.

The rue Percée(-Saint-André), recorded in 1262, between the rue Hautefeuille and the rue de la Harpe. When the boulevard Saint-Michel was cut through, the remaining stub became the impasse Hautefeuille. The label was added by hand.
In the 13th century the street of Eremburge de Brie, a name corrupted over time into Bout-de-Brie and Boutebrie; in the 14th century it was the street of the illuminators.
Opened around 1179, recorded as the 'vicus Serpentis' in 1180, probably for its winding course. In 1851 it absorbed the rue du Battoir-Saint-André. The label was added by hand.

The rue des Deux-Portes(-Saint-André), between the rue de la Harpe and the rue Hautefeuille, so named since 1450. It was destroyed when the boulevard Saint-Michel was cut through. The label was added by hand.
The hay street (foin), between the rue Saint-Jacques and the rue de la Harpe; in 1332 the rue de la Fennerie. It was destroyed by the boulevard Saint-Germain.

A road at the end of the 12th century, named after a shop sign showing a harp. Much of it was absorbed by the boulevard Saint-Michel in the 1850s; the surviving northern stretch is a lively street of the Latin Quarter.
The rue des Mathurins-Saint-Jacques, along the convent of the Mathurins. It was renamed in 1867 after Alexandre du Sommerard, founder of the Musée de Cluny.
In the 13th century the rue des Deux-Portes, then the rue Sorbonne around 1281, after the college; the poet Guillot called it 'rue aux Hoirs de Sabonnes' in 1300.
The rue des Poirées (leeks), recorded under other names in the 13th century. It disappeared when the Sorbonne was enlarged at the end of the 19th century.
Named after the convent of the Filles-Dieu, which was closed during the Revolution. It was renamed rue d'Alexandrie after Napoleon's capture of Alexandria.
Already called the rue Saint-Sauveur in 1285, after the church of Saint-Sauveur at its corner with the rue Saint-Denis.
The rue du Renard(-Saint-Sauveur), between the rue Saint-Denis and the rue Dussoubs, recorded in 1313 as the rue Percée. In 1868 it was joined to the rue Greneta.
The rue Beaurepaire, near Saint-Sauveur. In 1868 it was joined to the rue Greneta.
The rue des Deux-Portes(-Saint-Sauveur), closed by a gate at each end. It was renamed rue Dussoubs in 1881, after Denis Dussoubs, killed on the barricades in 1851.
In existence in 1390. Its original obscene name, rue Tire-Vit, was later softened to rue Tire-Boudin, and in 1809 it was renamed rue Marie-Stuart.
The street climbing the 'mont Orgueil', a small hill north of the Halles. It is still the market street of the quarter.
A rue Pavée (paved street) between the rue Dussoubs and the rue Montorgueil. It is now part of the rue Tiquetonne.

The rue de Bourgogne, opened on the grounds of the Hôtel de Bourgogne (or d'Artois) when it was broken up in 1543, so it was brand new when this map was made. Later the rue Françoise, now the rue Française.

The rue au Comte-d'Artois, named after the counts of Artois whose town house (the Hôtel de Bourgogne) stood here; the Tour Jean-sans-Peur survives from it. In 1792 it was joined to the rue Montorgueil.
In existence by 1250 as the rue Mauconseil ('bad counsel'). During the Revolution it was renamed rue Bonconseil.
In existence in the 12th century, the street of the truands — beggars and vagrants. Part of it disappeared in the rebuilding of the Halles in the 1970s.
Recorded in the tax roll of 1292, with names such as Maudestour or Maudétour, which became Mondétour. On this map it is 'Maude Tour'.
The cheese market street (Guillot in 1300 wrote 'Formagerie') in the Halles. It was destroyed in 1854 when Baltard's central market halls were built.

The street of the bishop's communal oven (four banal), in the 13th century the 'rue du Four de la Couture de l'Évêque'. It was renamed after the architect Vauvilliers; part of it was absorbed by the Halles.
A 13th-century street whose name comes from the priests (prouvaires) of Saint-Eustache. It once ran up to the church; part of it was absorbed by the Halles.
The second-hand clothes market (friperie) of the Halles. It was destroyed when Baltard's central market halls were built in the 1850s.
The linen market of the Halles, in existence in the early 13th century. Part of it disappeared in the rebuilding of the Halles in the 1970s.

A street near the Halles that bore this name from the early 13th century: tire-chape, 'pull-cape', from the second-hand dealers who tugged at passers-by. It was destroyed when the rue du Pont-Neuf was cut through.
The rue aux Chats, later the rue de la Limace, near the Halles. It has disappeared.
A street of the Halles quarter whose name may come from a family called Bourdon. Its southern stretches once had other names, such as rue Thibault-aux-Dés and rue de l'Arche-Marion.
In the mid-13th century the rue du Cerf, already called the rue de la Monnaie in 1387 after the royal mint that stood here until 1775.
In the 12th century the rue aux Moines de Joie-en-Val, later the rue des Deux-Portes and the rue de la Chapelle-aux-Orfèvres; it is named after the goldsmiths' chapel.
In existence in the 9th century. It was the main street from the Grand Châtelet to the church of Saint-Germain-l'Auxerrois; part of it was removed in 1882.
In 1300 simply the rue Pavée, in the 16th century the rue Pavée-d'Andouilles, later the rue Pavée-Saint-André. It was renamed in 1864 after the Séguier family of magistrates.
The rue du Battoir(-Saint-André), the 'Haulte Rue dite du Bastouer'. In 1851 it was joined to the rue Serpente.
In 1200 the rue d'Arondale (Hirondelle, swallow), in the old Laas quarter. Part of it was removed when the place Saint-Michel was created.
The street along the cemetery of Saint-André-des-Arts, in existence in the 12th century and called the rue des Sachettes in 1255. It was renamed after Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis.
In the 13th century the street of 'Gui le Queux among the Poitevins', a name shortened to rue des Poitevins. Its southern end was removed for the rue Danton in 1895.
In existence in 1252; its name may come from a tall tower or hall (haute feuille). The writer and philosopher Denis Diderot lived here.
Opened around 1179, recorded as the 'vicus Serpentis' in 1180, probably for its winding course.
A short street of the Latin Quarter, recorded in 1511 as the rue Jean-Sarrazin.
Called the rue des Cordèles (Cordeliers) by Guillot in 1300, after the Franciscan convent. It was renamed in 1790 after the medical school built on part of the convent.
Named after Roger Tiquetonne, a baker who lived here in 1399; the label shows the variant 'Quiquetonne'.
Built up between the present rue Rambuteau and rue Étienne-Marcel around 1200, leading out of the city to the Porte Montmartre and the hill of Montmartre.
The rue de la Plâtrière, a 13th-century street. Jean-Jacques Rousseau lived here in the 1770s; it was renamed after him in 1791.
In existence in the early 13th century, later called the ruelle du Séjour after a royal residence (séjour) of Charles V; the name was shortened to rue du Jour.
The rue des (Vieilles-)Étuves(-Saint-Honoré), the street of bathhouses, recorded in 1300. It was renamed after Henri Sauval, a 17th-century historian of Paris.
The rue d'Orléans(-Saint-Honoré), named after the Hôtel d'Orléans that stood nearby. It was destroyed in 1888 when the rue du Louvre was cut through.
The rue des Poulies, between the Louvre and the rue Saint-Honoré, named after the pulleys of a game played here. It was absorbed by the rue du Louvre.
The rue des Deux-Écus ('two shields', from a sign), near Saint-Eustache. It is now part of the rue Berger.

In 1269 the street of the abbot of Saint-Denis, then of the college of Saint-Denis that stood on it; it takes its present name from the Augustinian friary. Picasso painted Guernica in a studio on this street.
One of the main streets of the Left Bank, earlier called rue de Laas and rue Saint-Germain(-des-Prés), named after the church of Saint-André-des-Arts.
The rue du Paon(-Saint-André), renamed rue Larrey in 1851. It was destroyed when the boulevard Saint-Germain was cut through.

Successively the ruelle Saint-Sulpice, the ruelle du Champ-de-la-Foire (1517), the rue du Marché-aux-Chevaux and, from 1541, the rue de Tournon, after Cardinal François de Tournon, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. It leads up to the Luxembourg palace.
The rue des (Vieux-)Augustins, named after the Augustinian friars who were here before moving to the Left Bank in the 13th century. It is now the rue d'Argout and the rue Hérold.
Named after a chapel of Saint Mary of Egypt that stood here; 'l'Égyptienne' was corrupted into 'la Jussienne'.
Created at the end of the 13th century as the rue Pagevin, later the rue des Vieux-Augustins. It is now part of the rue d'Argout.
A cul-de-sac in 1298, turned into a through street when the Hôtel de Flandre was sold in 1543, just a few years before this map.
Fully built up by 1292, named after the Coquillier family; there was a postern gate of the same name in Philip Augustus's wall.
The rue de Grenelle(-Saint-Honoré), a 13th-century street; Ducerceau writes it 'Cernelles'. It was joined to the rue Jean-Jacques-Rousseau in 1868.
A very old road west from the Halles to the Porte Saint-Honoré. Its stretches once had separate names, such as the rue de la Chausseterie (hosiery) and the rue du Château-Fêtu.
In the 14th century the rue Richebourg, in 1376 the rue du Coq. It was renamed after Napoleon's victory at Marengo.
In existence in 1221 and named rue du Chantre (the cantor) from 1235. It was demolished to clear the surroundings of the Louvre.

Named after the Austrian (Autriche) who owned property here, corrupted into 'Autruche' (ostrich). Most of it disappeared when the Louvre was enlarged in 1664; the surviving part is the rue de l'Oratoire.
The rue du Champ-Fleuri ('flowery field'), near the Louvre, later the rue de la Bibliothèque. It disappeared when the Louvre was completed.
The rue Fromenteau (or Froidmanteau, 'cold coat'), near the Louvre, later the rue du Musée. It disappeared when the Louvre was completed.
The 'grant rue Saint-Sulpice', recorded as the rue du Colombier in 1292 after a dovecote of the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; it became the rue du Vieux-Colombier in the 17th century.
The road to the village of Vaugirard, the longest street in Paris today (4.3 km). On this map it starts at the Porte Saint-Michel.
In existence in the 14th century as the rue des Petits-Champs; the 'Croix' was a wayside cross at its corner with the rue Saint-Honoré.
The rue de Beauvais, near the Louvre, called 'Biauvoir' in the 13th century. It was demolished in 1806–1808 to clear the surroundings of the Louvre.
The rue Jean-Saint-Denis, a small street by the Louvre, later merged into a rue Pierre-Lescot that has also disappeared.
In 1212 the rue des Chanoines, from 1242 the rue Saint-Thomas-du-Louvre, after the collegiate church. It disappeared when the Louvre was enlarged in the 19th century.
The road from the Porte de Buci to the Pré-aux-Clercs and the Seine, recorded in 1259.
An ancient road to the villages of Issy and Sèvres, recorded as the 'vicus Furni' in 1261, after the communal oven of the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.
Probably the town house and college of the abbots of Saint-Denis, which gave the rue des Grands-Augustins its 13th-century name (rue de l'Abbé-de-Saint-Denis). It has disappeared.
The Petit Saint-Antoine, a house of the Hospitallers of Saint Anthony on the rue Saint-Antoine, who cared for sufferers of 'Saint Anthony's fire' (ergotism). It has disappeared.
A small church in front of Notre-Dame, one of the oldest in the Cité, linked to the Hôtel-Dieu. It was demolished in 1747 to enlarge the parvis.
A chapel on the rue Saint-Jacques dedicated to Saint Yves, patron saint of lawyers, founded in the 14th century by Breton students. It has disappeared.
The hospice of the Hospitallers of Altopascio (Haut-Pas) in Tuscany, who looked after pilgrims on the road to Santiago. Its chapel gave its name to the church of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas.
A wayside cross on the road east from Paris, near Charonne. The rue de la Croix-Faubin (11th arrondissement) keeps its name.
The suburb that grew up outside the Porte Saint-Victor, around the abbey of Saint-Victor.
The suburb outside the Porte Saint-Jacques, along the road to Orléans, with the hospice of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas and several convents.
The hay port on the Seine below the place de Grève, where boats unloaded hay for the city's horses.
The calf market, near the Grande Boucherie and the Grand Châtelet. The rue de la Vieille-Place-aux-Veaux, which kept its memory, disappeared in the 19th century.

The Grande Boucherie, the main butchers' market of Paris, next to the Grand Châtelet; its guild built the church of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie. It disappeared in the 19th century; the Tour Saint-Jacques stands nearby.
The pillory of the Halles, an octagonal tower with a turning wooden wheel in which offenders were exhibited to the crowd. It was demolished in the 18th century.
The grain hall of the medieval Halles. The later Halle au blé of the 18th century, now the Bourse de commerce, stands a short distance west.
The butchers' market of Beauvais at the Halles. It has disappeared.
The pillory of the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which had its own justice over the faubourg. It has disappeared.
A village east of Paris, here called 'Montreuil-sur-le-Bois', near the forest of Vincennes. It is now Montreuil, a large town in Seine-Saint-Denis.
A village on the Seine east of Paris, with riverside estates and, later, wine warehouses. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 and is now part of the 12th arrondissement.
A village at the confluence of the Seine and the Marne, with a country house of the archbishops of Paris. It is now part of Charenton-le-Pont.
A village on the Seine south-east of Paris, now Ivry-sur-Seine.
A village on the Seine south-east of Paris, now Vitry-sur-Seine.
A village on the road south from Paris, now Villejuif.
A village on the Bièvre south of Paris, now Gentilly. Part of its territory was annexed to Paris in 1860.
The ruined castle of Bicêtre, south of Paris. Louis XIII had a hospital for invalid soldiers built on the site; it later became the Hôpital Bicêtre, in Le Kremlin-Bicêtre.
A village on a hill north-east of Paris, whose springs supplied the city's fountains. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 (19th and 20th arrondissements).
A village east of Paris, now Bagnolet.
A village east of Paris, on the site of a Merovingian royal residence. It was absorbed into the faubourg Saint-Antoine and is now a quarter of the 12th arrondissement.
A hamlet north-east of the city, outside the wall. Its name survives in the rue Popincourt and the Popincourt quarter of the 11th arrondissement.
A hamlet on the road to Belleville, known for its taverns: just outside the city, wine escaped the city's toll. It is now the area around the rue du Faubourg-du-Temple and Belleville.

The marais, market gardens on the old marshland north of the city wall, where vegetables for Paris were grown. Today the area is part of the 10th arrondissement; the Marais district inside the walls has the same origin.
The suburb along the road north from the Porte Saint-Martin, around the church of Saint-Laurent and the Saint-Laurent fair.
The suburb along the road north from the Porte Saint-Denis towards the abbey of Saint-Denis. The rue du Faubourg-Saint-Denis follows its main street.

A suburb north of the city walls, the Villeneuve-sur-Gravois, where the church of Notre-Dame-de-Bonne-Nouvelle was built in the 16th century. It was destroyed during the siege of 1591 and later rebuilt; it is the Bonne-Nouvelle quarter of today.
A hamlet on the north side of the hill of Montmartre, now the Clignancourt quarter of the 18th arrondissement.
The hill north of Paris with its village and the Benedictine abbey of Montmartre. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 and is now the 18th arrondissement.
A fortified farm north-west of the city, belonging to the bishops of Paris and later the Hôtel-Dieu, on a stream of the same name. The rue de la Grange-Batelière (9th arrondissement) keeps its name.

The suburb that grew up around the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés outside Philip Augustus's wall, with the Saint-Germain fair. In the 17th and 18th centuries it became the most aristocratic quarter of Paris.
A hamlet north-west of the city with a manor house, later known for its open-air taverns. It is now part of the 9th arrondissement.
The suburb along the road west from the Porte Saint-Honoré. The rue du Faubourg-Saint-Honoré follows its main street; the Élysée palace stands on it.
A village west of the city belonging to the bishop of Paris, hence its name (the bishop's town). The rue de la Ville-l'Évêque, near the Madeleine, keeps its name.
A village on the road west from Paris, with a leper house. It was absorbed into the faubourg Saint-Honoré; the church of Saint-Philippe-du-Roule keeps its name.
A village on the hill west of Paris above the Seine. It was annexed in 1860; the Palais de Chaillot stands at the top of the hill.
A village west of Paris on the Seine, later a favourite country retreat of writers such as Molière and Boileau. It was annexed to Paris in 1860 and is now part of the 16th arrondissement.
